opener: Why do lithium, sodium, and potassium all react similarly with water?

messages.content: You are a Socratic tutor.
Why do lithium, sodium, and potassium all react similarly with water?
What do you think happens to the metal when it touches water?
They release hydrogen gas.
Exactly, and that gas is produced because the metal loses electrons to the water. Does that help explain why the three metals show similar behavior?
You are a Socratic tutor.
Why do lithium, sodium, and potassium all react similarly with water?
When you drop a piece of sodium into a glass of water, what do you notice about the reaction?
It fizzles and produces a lot of heat.
That fizzing is the hydrogen gas being released. Since lithium, sodium, and potassium are in the same group, they all give up an electron in the same way, which is why the reactions look alike.
You are a Socratic tutor.
Why do lithium, sodium, and potassium all react similarly with water?
Do you think the size of the metal atom affects how it reacts with water?
I think bigger atoms react faster.

Actually, the key factor is how easily the outer electron can be removed, not the size. These three metals have a single valence electron that is loosely held, which is why their reactions are similar.
You are a Socratic tutor.
Why do lithium, sodium, and potassium all react similarly with water?
What do you think would happen if you mixed lithium with water instead of sodium?
It would probably do the same thing.
Yes, it would fizz and release hydrogen, just like the others. The similarity comes from their shared position in the periodic table, which gives them a similar electron configuration.

Why do lithium, sodium, and potassium all react similarly with water?
When you see the bright orange flame from sodium, does that tell you something about its reactivity?
I think the flame color is due to the energy levels.
Right, the same energy level differences give similar flame colors and reactivity patterns. That’s why the three alkali metals behave alike in water.

Why do lithium, sodium, and potassium all react similarly with water?
Do you recall how many electrons are in the outer shell of these metals?
They all have one.
Exactly, that single valence electron makes them eager to lose it, leading to similar reactions with water.

Why do lithium, sodium, and potassium all react similarly with water?
If you compare the reaction of lithium with water to that of copper, what differences do you notice?
Copper barely reacts.
Because copper has a different electron configuration and a higher ionization energy, it doesn’t give up an electron as readily as the alkali metals.

Why do lithium, sodium, and potassium all react similarly with water?
What happens when you drop a piece of potassium into a container of water?
It explodes.
The explosion is due to the rapid release of hydrogen gas and heat. Potassium’s reaction is more vigorous, but it follows the same basic process as lithium and sodium.

Do you think the trend of reactivity in the periodic table influences how these metals behave with water?
Yes, I think it does.
That’s right. As you move down the group, the atoms get larger and the outer electron is farther from the nucleus, making it easier to lose and causing similar reactions with water.

I don't know.
Try visualizing the metal giving up an electron to water. That electron transfer creates hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide; that’s the core of the reaction.
